claim: Recombinant R. rubrum encapsulin nanocompartments were produced in E. coli by co-expression of encapsulin (Rru_A0974) and EncFtn (Rru_A0973) proteins.
source: We produced recombinant R. rubrum encapsulin nanocompartments in E. coli by co-expression of the encapsulin (Rru_A0974) and EncFtn (Rru_A0973) proteins, and purified these by sucrose gradient ultra-centrifugation (Figure 1A) (Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure of producing recombinant nanocompartments and cites a reference for the purification method.

claim: When expressed in isolation, the R. rubrum encapsulin protein forms empty compartments with an average diameter of 24 nm.
source: TEM imaging of uranyl acetate-stained samples revealed that, when expressed in isolation, the encapsulin protein forms empty compartments with an average diameter of 24 nm (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A/C), consistent with the appearance and size of the T. maritima encapsulin (Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging data presented in figures and is compared to published data on T. maritima encapsulin.

claim: Co-expression of encapsulin and EncFtn resulted in 24 nm compartments with regions in the center that exclude stain, consistent with the presence of EncFtn within the encapsulin shell.
source: Protein purified from co-expression of the encapsulin and EncFtn resulted in 24 nm compartments with regions in the center that exclude stain, consistent with the presence of the EncFtn within the encapsulin shell (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B/C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging data showing stain exclusion in the center of compartments.

claim: The high molecular weight peak of EncFtn from size-exclusion chromatography was partially resistant to SDS and heat-induced denaturation.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of fractions from these peaks showed that the high molecular weight peak was partially resistant to SDS and heat-induced denaturation; in contrast, the low molecular weight peak was consistent with monomeric mass of 13 kDa (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE analysis data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: ICP-MS analysis showed 100 times more iron in the oligomeric fraction of EncFtn than in the monomer.
source: Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) analysis of the SEC fractions showed 100 times more iron in the oligomeric fraction than the monomer (Figure 2A, blue scatter points; Table 1), suggesting that EncFtn oligomerization is associated with iron binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP-MS data presented in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: SEC-MALLS analysis gave calculated molecular weights consistent with a decamer for the high molecular weight peak and a monomer for the low molecular weight peak of EncFtn.
source: Size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALLS) analysis of samples taken from each peak gave calculated molecular weights consistent with a decamer for the high molecular weight peak and a monomer for the low molecular weight peak (Figure 2C, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALLS data presented in Figure 2C and Table 2.

claim: The decamer to monomer ratio in EncFtnsH purified from cells grown in iron-supplemented media was 4.5, while that from iron-free media was 0.11.
source: The decamer to monomer ratio in the sample purified from cells grown in iron-supplemented media was 4.5, while that from the iron-free media was 0.11, suggesting that iron induces the oligomerization of EncFtnsH in vivo (Figure 3A, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by gel filtration data presented in Figure 3A and Table 3.

claim: Of the metals tested, only Fe2+, Zn2+ and Co2+ induced the formation of significant amounts of the EncFtnsH decamer.
source: Of the metals tested, only Fe2+, Zn2+ and Co2+ induced the formation of significant amounts of the decamer (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1/2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analytical SEC and native PAGE data presented in figures.

claim: Fe3+ in the form of FeCl3 does not induce multimerization of EncFtnsH.
source: While Fe2+ induces the multimerization of EncFtnsH, Fe3+ in the form of FeCl3 does not have this effect on the protein, highlighting the apparent preference this protein has for the ferrous form of iron.
evidence: The claim is supported by analytical SEC data comparing the effects of Fe2+ and Fe3+.

claim: The crystal structure of EncFtnsH was determined by molecular replacement to 2.0 Å resolution.
source: We determined the crystal structure of EncFtnsH by molecular replacement to 2.0 Å resolution (see Table 1 for X-ray data collection and refinement statistics).
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data and refinement statistics in Table 4.

claim: The crystallographic asymmetric unit of EncFtnsH contained thirty monomers arranged as three identical annular decamers, each with D5 symmetry.
source: The crystallographic asymmetric unit contained thirty monomers of EncFtn with visible electron density for residues 7 – 96 in each chain. The protein chains were arranged as three identical annular decamers, each with D5 symmetry.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data analysis.

claim: The EncFtnsH decamer has a diameter of 7 nm and thickness of 4 nm.
source: The decamer has a diameter of 7 nm and thickness of 4 nm (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural measurements from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The monomer of EncFtn has an N-terminal 310-helix that precedes two 4 nm long antiparallel α-helices arranged with their long axes at 25° to each other.
source: The monomer of EncFtn has an N-terminal 310-helix that precedes two 4 nm long antiparallel α-helices arranged with their long axes at 25° to each other; these helices are followed by a shorter 1.4 nm helix projecting at 70° from α2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Diffraction data collected at the experimentally determined iron absorption edge (1.74 Å) showed two 10-sigma peaks between residues Glu32, Glu62 and His65 of two adjacent chains, and a 5-sigma peak between residues Glu31 and Glu34.
source: Informed by the ICP-MS data indicating the presence of iron in the protein we collected diffraction data at the experimentally determined iron absorption edge (1.74 Å) and calculated an anomalous difference Fourier map using this data. Inspection of this map showed two 10-sigma peaks between residues Glu32, Glu62 and His65 of two adjacent chains, and a statistically smaller 5-sigma peak between residues Glu31 and Glu34 of the two chains.
evidence: The claim is supported by anomalous diffraction data analysis.

claim: Modeling metal ions into the anomalous peaks and refinement of the anomalous scattering parameters allowed identification of two iron ions and a calcium ion in the EncFtnsH structure.
source: Modeling metal ions into these peaks and refinement of the anomalous scattering parameters allowed us to identify these as two iron ions and a calcium ion respectively (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic modeling and refinement data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The di-iron center in EncFtnsH has an Fe-Fe distance of 3.5 Å.
source: This di-iron center has an Fe-Fe distance of 3.5 Å, Fe-Glu-O distances between 2.3 and 2.5 Å, and Fe-His-N distances of 2.5 Å (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural measurements from the crystal structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The coordination geometry of the di-iron center in EncFtnsH is consistent with the di-nuclear ferroxidase center (FOC) found in ferritin.
source: This coordination geometry is consistent with the di-nuclear ferroxidase center (FOC) found in ferritin (Bertini et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published ferritin structures.

claim: The FOC in EncFtnsH was fully occupied with iron in the final structure, despite no additional iron being added to crystallization trials.
source: It is interesting to note that although we did not add any additional iron to the crystallization trials, the FOC was fully occupied with iron in the final structure, implying that this site has a very high affinity for iron.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data and implies high iron affinity based on observation.

claim: Structural alignment of the di-iron binding site of EncFtnsH to the FOC of Pseudo-nitzschia multiseries ferritin reveals a striking similarity between the metal binding sites.
source: Structural alignment of the di-iron binding site of EncFtnsH to the FOC of Pseudo-nitzschia multiseries ferritin (PmFtn, PDB ID: 4ITW) reveals a striking similarity between the metal binding sites of EncFtnsH and the classical ferritins (Pfaffen et al., 2013) (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6A and cited reference.

claim: Native MS analysis of EncFtnsH produced in minimal media displayed a charge state distribution consistent with an EncFtnsH monomer with an average neutral mass of 13,194 Da.
source: Native MS analysis of EncFtnsH produced in this way displayed a charge state distribution consistent with an EncFtnsH monomer (blue circles, Figure 7A1) with an average neutral mass of 13,194 Da, in agreement with the predicted mass of the EncFtnsH protein (13,194.53 Da).
evidence: The claim is supported by native mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7A1.

claim: Titration with Fe2+ resulted in the appearance of a new charge state distribution consistent with an EncFtnsH decameric assembly (+22 to +26; 132.65 kDa).
source: Titration with Fe2+ directly before native MS analysis resulted in the appearance of a new charge state distribution, consistent with an EncFtnsH decameric assembly (+22 to +26; 132.65 kDa) (Figure 7A2/3).
evidence: The claim is supported by native mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7A2/3.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis assigned iron-loading in the EncFtnsH complex to between 10 and 15 Fe ions per decamer.
source: After instrument optimization, the mass resolving power achieved was sufficient to assign iron-loading in the complex to between 10 and 15 Fe ions per decamer (Figure 7B, inset top right), consistent with the presence of 10 irons in the FOC and the coordination of iron in the Glu31/34-site occupied by calcium in the crystal structure (Δmass observed ~0.67 kDa).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-resolution mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Ion mobility analysis of the EncFtnsH decameric assembly suggested that it consists of a single conformation with a collision cross section (CCS) of 58.2 nm2.
source: Ion mobility analysis of the EncFtnsH decameric assembly, collected with minimal collisional activation, suggested that it consists of a single conformation with a collision cross section (CCS) of 58.2 nm2 (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ion mobility mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The calculated CCS from the crystal structure of the EncFtnsH decamer is 58.7 nm2.
source: This observation is in agreement with the calculated CCS of 58.7 nm2derived from our crystal structure of the EncFtnsH decamer (Marklund, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of the crystal structure using cited software.

claim: IM-MS measurements of monomeric EncFtnsH at pH 8.0 revealed that the metal-free protein monomer exists in a wide range of charge states (+6 to +16) and adopts many conformations with collision cross sections ranging from 12 nm2 to 26 nm2.
source: By contrast, IM-MS measurements of the monomeric EncFtnsH at pH 8.0 under the same instrumental conditions revealed that the metal-free protein monomer exists in a wide range of charge states (+6 to +16) and adopts many conformations in the gas phase with collision cross sections ranging from 12 nm2 to 26 nm2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ion mobility mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wide range of charge states and conformations of monomeric EncFtnsH are indicative of an unstructured protein with little secondary or tertiary structure.
source: These observations are indicative of an unstructured protein with little secondary or tertiary structure (Beveridge et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by interpretation of IM-MS data and cited reference on protein structure characterization.

claim: CID of the EncFtnsH decamer resulted in the appearance of a dimeric EncFtnsH subcomplex containing 0, 1, or 2 iron ions.
source: For EncFtnsH, this atypical dissociation pathway was clearly evident; CID of the EncFtnsH decamer resulted in the appearance of a dimeric EncFtnsH subcomplex containing 0, 1, or 2 iron ions (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by collision-induced dissociation mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: EncFtnsH showed no peroxidase activity when assayed with the substrate ortho-phenylenediamine.
source: Unlike the Dps family of ferritin-like proteins, EncFtn showed no peroxidase activity when assayed with the substrate ortho-phenylenediamine (Pesek et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by peroxidase assay data and comparison to Dps proteins.

claim: The ferroxidase activity of EncFtnsH was measured by recording the progress curve of Fe2+ oxidation to Fe3+ at 315 nm after addition of 20 and 100 µM Fe2+.
source: The ferroxidase activity of EncFtnsH was measured by recording the progress curve of Fe2+ oxidation to Fe3+ at 315 nm after addition of 20 and 100 µM Fe2+ (2 and 10 times molar ratio Fe2+/FOC).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used to measure ferroxidase activity.

claim: In ferroxidase assays, the rate of oxidation by EncFtnsH was faster than background oxidation of Fe2+ by molecular oxygen.
source: In both experiments the rate of oxidation was faster than background oxidation of Fe2+ by molecular oxygen, and was highest for 100 µM Fe2+ (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ferroxidase assay data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Recombinant EncFtnsH acts as an active ferroxidase enzyme.
source: These data show that recombinant EncFtnsH acts as an active ferroxidase enzyme.
evidence: The claim is supported by ferroxidase assay data.

claim: When compared to apoferritin, EncFtnsH oxidized Fe2+ at a slower rate and the reaction did not run to completion over 1800 s.
source: When compared to apoferritin, EncFtnsH oxidized Fe2+ at a slower rate and the reaction did not run to completion over the 1800 s of the experiment.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ferroxidase assay data between EncFtnsH and apoferritin.

claim: Recombinant encapsulin, when assayed alone, did not display ferroxidase activity above background Fe2+ oxidation.
source: We also performed these assays on purified recombinant encapsulin; which, when assayed alone, did not display ferroxidase activity above background Fe2+ oxidation (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ferroxidase assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Complexes of the full EncFtn encapsulin nanocompartment (EncFtn-Enc) displayed ferroxidase activity comparable to apoferritin without the formation of precipitates.
source: In contrast, complexes of the full EncFtn encapsulin nanocompartment (i.e. the EncFtn-Enc protein complex) displayed ferroxidase activity comparable to apoferritin without the formation of precipitates (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ferroxidase assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The EncFtnsH reaction mixture showed the formation of large, irregular electron-dense precipitates in TEM analysis.
source: The EncFtnsH reaction mixture showed the formation of large, irregular electron-dense precipitates (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of Fe2+ to the EncFtn-Enc nanocompartment resulted in small, highly regular, electron dense particles of approximately 5 nm in diameter.
source: In contrast, addition of Fe2+ to the EncFtn-Enc nanocompartment resulted in small, highly regular, electron dense particles of approximately 5 nm in diameter (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C); we interpret these observations as controlled mineralization of iron within the nanocompartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and interpreted as controlled mineralization.

claim: The EncFtnsH decamer binds a maximum of around 48 iron ions before excess iron induces protein precipitation.
source: In this assay, the EncFtnsH decamer binds a maximum of around 48 iron ions before excess iron induces protein precipitation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ferrozine assay data measuring iron loading capacity.

claim: The encapsulin shell protein can sequester about 2200 iron ions before significant protein loss occurs.
source: The encapsulin shell protein can sequester about 2200 iron ions before significant protein loss occurs, and the reconstituted EncFtn-Enc nanocompartment sequestered about 4150 iron ions.
evidence: The claim is supported by ferrozine assay data measuring iron loading capacity.

claim: The reconstituted EncFtn-Enc nanocompartment sequestered about 4150 iron ions.
source: The encapsulin shell protein can sequester about 2200 iron ions before significant protein loss occurs, and the reconstituted EncFtn-Enc nanocompartment sequestered about 4150 iron ions.
evidence: The claim is supported by ferrozine assay data measuring iron loading capacity.

claim: The EncFtn-Enc nanocompartment sequestered significantly more iron than the apoferritin used in the assay, which sequesters approximately 570 iron ions.
source: This latter result is significantly more than the apoferritin used in our assay, which sequesters approximately 570 iron ions in this assay (Figure 8C, Table 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of iron loading capacity data shown in Figure 8C and Table 5.

claim: The E32A and E62A mutants of EncFtnsH eluted from SEC at a volume consistent with the decameric form, with a small proportion of monomer.
source: The E32A and E62A mutants eluted from SEC at a volume consistent with the decameric form of EncFtnsH, with a small proportion of monomer; the H65A mutant eluted at a volume consistent with the monomeric form of EncFtnsH (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The H65A mutant of EncFtnsH eluted at a volume consistent with the monomeric form.
source: The E32A and E62A mutants eluted from SEC at a volume consistent with the decameric form of EncFtnsH, with a small proportion of monomer; the H65A mutant eluted at a volume consistent with the monomeric form of EncFtnsH (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 9.

claim: For all EncFtnsH mutants studied, no change in oligomerization state was apparent upon addition of Fe2+ in vitro.
source: For all of the mutants studied, no change in oligomerization state was apparent upon addition of Fe2+ in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by analytical SEC data on mutant proteins.

claim: Native mass spectrometry showed that both the E32A and E62A mutants displayed charge state distributions consistent with decamers, even in the absence of Fe2+.
source: Both the E32A mutant and E62A mutant displayed charge state distributions consistent with decamers, even in the absence of Fe2+. This gas-phase observation is consistent with SEC measurements, which indicate both of these variants were also decamers in solution.
evidence: The claim is supported by native mass spectrometry data and SEC measurements.

claim: MS analysis of the H65A mutant showed it is present as a monomer, with a minor population of dimeric H65A also observed.
source: In contrast to the glutamic acid mutants, MS analysis of the H65A mutant is similar to wild-type apo-EncFtnsH and is present as a monomer; interestingly a minor population of dimeric H65A was also observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by native mass spectrometry data.

claim: The crystal packing of all EncFtnsH mutants is essentially isomorphous to the wild-type EncFtnsH structure.
source: The crystal packing of all of the mutants in this study is essentially isomorphous to the EncFtnsH structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic analysis of mutant structures.

claim: All EncFtnsH mutants display the same decameric arrangement in the crystals as the wild-type structure.
source: All of the mutants display the same decameric arrangement in the crystals as the EncFtnsH structure, and the monomers superimpose with an average RMSDCα of less than 0.2 Å.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic analysis and structural superimposition.

claim: Mutagenesis of E32A and H65A reduces the ferroxidase activity of EncFtnsH by about 40%-55%.
source: Mutagenesis of E32A and H65A reduces the activity of EncFtnsH by about 40%-55%; the E62A mutant completely abrogates activity, presumably through the loss of the bridging coordination for the formation of the di-nuclear iron center of the FOC (Figure 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by ferroxidase assay data shown in Figure 12.

claim: The E62A mutant completely abrogates ferroxidase activity of EncFtnsH.
source: Mutagenesis of E32A and H65A reduces the activity of EncFtnsH by about 40%-55%; the E62A mutant completely abrogates activity, presumably through the loss of the bridging coordination for the formation of the di-nuclear iron center of the FOC (Figure 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by ferroxidase assay data shown in Figure 12 and inferred mechanism.

claim: EncFtn adopts an open decameric structure that is topologically distinct from other ferritins.
source: EncFtn adopts an open decameric structure that is topologically distinct from other ferritins.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure determination and comparison to other ferritins.

claim: While EncFtn acts as a ferroxidase, it cannot mineralize iron.
source: While EncFtn acts as a ferroxidase, it cannot mineralize iron.
evidence: The claim is supported by ferroxidase assay data and TEM analysis showing lack of controlled mineralization by EncFtn alone.

claim: The encapsulin shell associates with iron, but is not enzymatically active.
source: Conversely, the encapsulin shell associates with iron, but is not enzymatically active, and we demonstrate that EncFtn must be housed within the encapsulin for iron storage.
evidence: The claim is supported by ferroxidase assay data showing no enzymatic activity and iron loading capacity data.

claim: EncFtn must be housed within the encapsulin for iron storage.
source: Conversely, the encapsulin shell associates with iron, but is not enzymatically active, and we demonstrate that EncFtn must be housed within the encapsulin for iron storage.
evidence: The claim is supported by combined data from ferroxidase assays, TEM analysis, and iron loading capacity experiments.

claim: This encapsulin nanocompartment is widely distributed in bacteria and archaea.
source: This encapsulin nanocompartment is widely distributed in bacteria and archaea and represents a distinct class of iron storage system, where the oxidation and mineralization of iron are distributed between two proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and literature on encapsulin distribution.

claim: The encapsulin nanocompartment represents a distinct class of iron storage system, where the oxidation and mineralization of iron are distributed between two proteins.
source: This encapsulin nanocompartment is widely distributed in bacteria and archaea and represents a distinct class of iron storage system, where the oxidation and mineralization of iron are distributed between two proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined structural and biochemical characterization showing functional separation between EncFtn and encapsulin.

claim: Encapsulin nanocompartments share a common architecture, comprising an icosahedral shell formed by the oligomeric assembly of encapsulin protein that is structurally related to the HK97 bacteriophage capsid protein gp5.
source: They share a common architecture, comprising an icosahedral shell formed by the oligomeric assembly of a protein, encapsulin, that is structurally related to the HK97 bacteriophage capsid protein gp5 (Helgstrand et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited structural studies on encapsulins and HK97.

claim: The Pyrococcus furiosus and Myxococcus xanthus encapsulin shell-proteins form 32 nm icosahedra with 180 subunits.
source: In contrast, both the Pyrococcus furiosus (Akita et al., 2007) and Myxococcus xanthus (McHugh et al., 2014) encapsulin shell-proteins form 32 nm icosahedra with 180 subunits; while the Thermotoga maritima (Sutter et al., 2008) encapsulin is smaller still with a 25 nm, 60-subunit icosahedron.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited structural studies on different encapsulins.

claim: The Thermotoga maritima encapsulin forms a 25 nm, 60-subunit icosahedron.
source: In contrast, both the Pyrococcus furiosus (Akita et al., 2007) and Myxococcus xanthus (McHugh et al., 2014) encapsulin shell-proteins form 32 nm icosahedra with 180 subunits; while the Thermotoga maritima (Sutter et al., 2008) encapsulin is smaller still with a 25 nm, 60-subunit icosahedron.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited structural study on T. maritima encapsulin.

claim: The high structural similarity of encapsulin shell-proteins to gp5 suggests a common evolutionary origin for these proteins.
source: The high structural similarity of the encapsulin shell-proteins to gp5 suggests a common evolutionary origin for these proteins (McHugh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on structural similarity and is supported by cited reference.

claim: The genes encoding encapsulin proteins are found downstream of genes for dye-dependent peroxidase (DyP) family enzymes or encapsulin-associated ferritins (EncFtn).
source: The genes encoding encapsulin proteins are found downstream of genes for dye-dependent peroxidase (DyP) family enzymes (Roberts et al., 2011), or encapsulin-associated ferritins (EncFtn) (He and Marles-Wright, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited genomic studies.

claim: Enzymes in the DyP family are active against polyphenolic compounds such as azo dyes and lignin breakdown products.
source: Enzymes in the DyP family are active against polyphenolic compounds such as azo dyes and lignin breakdown products; although their physiological function and natural substrates are not known (Roberts et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited biochemical studies on DyP enzymes.

claim: The physiological function and natural substrates of DyP family enzymes are not known.
source: Enzymes in the DyP family are active against polyphenolic compounds such as azo dyes and lignin breakdown products; although their physiological function and natural substrates are not known (Roberts et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference indicating lack of knowledge.

claim: Ferritin family proteins are found in all kingdoms and have a wide range of activities, including ribonucleotide reductase, protecting DNA from oxidative damage, and iron storage.
source: Ferritin family proteins are found in all kingdoms and have a wide range of activities, including ribonucleotide reductase (Aberg et al., 1993), protecting DNA from oxidative damage (Grant et al., 1998), and iron storage (Bradley et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references on ferritin family functions.

claim: Classical iron storage ferritin nanocages are found in all kingdoms and are essential in eukaryotes.
source: The classical iron storage ferritin nanocages are found in all kingdoms and are essential in eukaryotes; they play a central role in iron homeostasis, where they protect the cell from toxic free Fe2+ by oxidizing it and storing the resulting Fe3+ as ferrihydrite minerals within their central cavity.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge on ferritin distribution and function.

claim: Classical ferritins protect the cell from toxic free Fe2+ by oxidizing it and storing the resulting Fe3+ as ferrihydrite minerals within their central cavity.
source: The classical iron storage ferritin nanocages are found in all kingdoms and are essential in eukaryotes; they play a central role in iron homeostasis, where they protect the cell from toxic free Fe2+ by oxidizing it and storing the resulting Fe3+ as ferrihydrite minerals within their central cavity.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge on ferritin function.

claim: The encapsulin-associated enzymes are sequestered within the icosahedral shell through interactions between the shell's inner surface and a short localization sequence (Gly-Ser-Leu-Lys) appended to their C-termini.
source: The encapsulin-associated enzymes are sequestered within the icosahedral shell through interactions between the shell's inner surface and a short localization sequence (Gly-Ser-Leu-Lys) appended to their C-termini (Sutter et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The encapsulin localization motif is well-conserved, and the addition of this sequence to heterologous proteins is sufficient to direct them to the interior of encapsulins.
source: This motif is well-conserved, and the addition of this sequence to heterologous proteins is sufficient to direct them to the interior of encapsulins (Rurup et al., 2014; 2015; Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies on protein targeting to encapsulins.

claim: The Myxococcus xanthus encapsulin sequesters a number of different EncFtn proteins and acts as an 'iron-megastore' to protect these bacteria from oxidative stress.
source: A recent study of the Myxococcus xanthus encapsulin showed that it sequesters a number of different EncFtn proteins and acts as an 'iron-megastore' to protect these bacteria from oxidative stress (McHugh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited study on M. xanthus encapsulin function.

claim: At 32 nm in diameter, the M. xanthus encapsulin is much larger than other members of the ferritin superfamily and is capable of sequestering up to ten times more iron than classical ferritins.
source: At 32 nm in diameter, it is much larger than other members of the ferritin superfamily, such as the 12 nm 24-subunit classical ferritin nanocage and the 8 nm 12-subunit Dps (DNA-binding protein from starved cells) complex (Grant et al., 1998; Andrews, 2010); and is thus capable of sequestering up to ten times more iron than these ferritins (McHugh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited structural and functional studies comparing encapsulin to other ferritins.

claim: The primary sequences of EncFtn proteins have Glu-X-X-His metal coordination sites, which are shared features of the ferritin family proteins.
source: The primary sequences of EncFtn proteins have Glu-X-X-His metal coordination sites, which are shared features of the ferritin family proteins (Andrews, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and cited reference on ferritin family characteristics.

claim: Secondary structure prediction identifies two major α-helical regions in EncFtn proteins, in contrast to other members of the ferritin superfamily, which have four major α-helices.
source: Secondary structure prediction identifies two major α-helical regions in these proteins; this is in contrast to other members of the ferritin superfamily, which have four major α-helices (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by secondary structure prediction analysis and comparison to known ferritin structures.

claim: The Rhodospirillum rubrum EncFtn protein (Rru_A0973) shares 33% protein sequence identity with the M. xanthus (MXAN_4464), 53% with the T. maritima (Tmari_0787), and 29% with the P. furiosus (PF1192) homologues.
source: The Rhodospirillum rubrum EncFtn protein (Rru_A0973) shares 33% protein sequence identity with the M. xanthus (MXAN_4464), 53% with the T. maritima (Tmari_0787), and 29% with the P. furiosus (PF1192) homologues.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The GXXH motifs are strictly conserved in EncFtn proteins from R. rubrum, M. xanthus, T. maritima, and P. furiosus.
source: The GXXH motifs are strictly conserved in each of these species (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The four-helical fold of the classical ferritins may have arisen through gene duplication of an ancestor of EncFtn.
source: From this analysis, we propose that the four-helical fold of the classical ferritins may have arisen through gene duplication of an ancestor of EncFtn.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on phylogenetic analysis and structural comparison.

claim: Gene duplication linking the C-terminal region of one EncFtn monomer to the N-terminus of another would stabilize the four-helix bundle fold within a single polypeptide chain.
source: This gene duplication would result in the C-terminal region of one EncFtn monomer being linked to the N-terminus of another and thus stabilizing the four-helix bundle fold within a single polypeptide chain (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic proposal based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Linking the EncFtn protein together through gene duplication would relax the requirement for the maintenance of a symmetrical FOC and provide a path to the diversity in active-site residues seen across the ferritin family.
source: Linking the protein together in this way relaxes the requirement for the maintenance of a symmetrical FOC and thus provides a path to the diversity in active-site residues seen across the ferritin family (Figure 6A, residues Glu95, Gln128 and Glu131 in PmFtn, Supplementary file 1) (Andrews, 2010; Lundin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is an evolutionary inference based on structural and sequence analysis.

claim: The quaternary arrangement of classical ferritins into an octahedral nanocage and Dps into a dodecamer is absolutely required for their function as iron storage compartments.
source: The quaternary arrangement of classical ferritins into an octahedral nanocage and Dps into a dodecamer is absolutely required for their function as iron storage compartments (Chasteen and Harrison, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference on ferritin structure-function relationships.

claim: The oxidation and mineralization of iron must be spatially separated from the host cytosol to prevent the formation of damaging hydroxyl radicals in the Fenton and Haber-Weiss reactions.
source: The oxidation and mineralization of iron must be spatially separated from the host cytosol to prevent the formation of damaging hydroxyl radicals in the Fenton and Haber-Weiss reactions (Honarmand Ebrahimi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference on iron chemistry and oxidative damage.

claim: In all ferritins, spatial separation of iron oxidation is achieved by confining the oxidation of iron to the interior of the protein complex.
source: This is achieved in all ferritins by confining the oxidation of iron to the interior of the protein complex, thus achieving sequestration of the Fe3+ mineralization product.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge on ferritin function.

claim: A structural alignment of the FOC of EncFtn with classical ferritin PmFtn shows that the central ring of EncFtn corresponds to the external surface of ferritin, while the outer circumference of EncFtn is congruent with the inner mineralization surface of ferritin.
source: A structural alignment of the FOC of EncFtn with the classical ferritin PmFtn shows that the central ring of EncFtn corresponds to the external surface of ferritin, while the outer circumference of EncFtn is congruent with the inner mineralization surface of ferritin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural alignment analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ferroxidase center of EncFtn faces in the opposite direction relative to the classical ferritins and is essentially inside out regarding iron storage space.
source: This overlay highlights the fact that the ferroxidase center of EncFtn faces in the opposite direction relative to the classical ferritins and is essentially inside out regarding iron storage space (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, boxed region).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The position of the calcium ion coordinated by Glu31 and Glu34 in the EncFtnsH structure suggests an entry site to channel metal ions into the FOC.
source: Furthermore, the position of the calcium ion coordinated by Glu31 and Glu34 seen in the EncFtnsH structure suggests an entry site to channel metal ions into the FOC; we propose that this site binds hydrated iron ions in vivo and acts as a selectivity filter and gate for the FOC (Haldar et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on structural analysis and cited reference on metal ion channels.

claim: The constellation of charged residues on the outer circumference of EncFtn (His57, Glu61 and Glu64) could function as the exit portal and mineralization site.
source: The constellation of charged residues on the outer circumference of EncFtn (His57, Glu61 and Glu64) could function in the same way as the residues lining the mineralization surface within the classical ferritin nanocage (Le Brun et al., 2010), and given their proximity to the FOC these sites may be the exit portal and mineralization site (Honarmand Ebrahimi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on structural analysis and cited references on ferritin mineralization.

claim: The absolute requirement for spatial separation of oxidation and mineralization in ferritins suggests that the EncFtn family proteins are not capable of storing iron minerals due to the absence of an enclosed compartment in their structure.
source: The absolute requirement for the spatial separation of oxidation and mineralization in ferritins suggests that the EncFtn family proteins are not capable of storing iron minerals due to the absence of an enclosed compartment in their structure (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on structural analysis and ferritin function principles.

claim: Docking the decamer structure of EncFtnsH into the pentamer of the T. maritima encapsulin shows that the position of the C-terminal extensions are consistent with the localization sequences seen bound to the encapsulin protein.
source: Docking the decamer structure of EncFtnsH into the pentamer of the T. maritima encapsulin Tmari_0786 (PDB ID: 3DKT) (Sutter et al., 2008) shows that the position of the C-terminal extensions of our EncFtnsH structure are consistent with the localization sequences seen bound to the encapsulin protein (Figure 14A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural docking analysis shown in Figure 14A.

claim: The EncFtn decamer is the physiological state of this protein.
source: Thus, it appears that the EncFtn decamer is the physiological state of this protein.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on structural docking and biochemical data.

claim: The arrangement of EncFtn in the encapsulin positions the central ring of EncFtn directly above the pore at the five-fold symmetry axis of the encapsulin shell.
source: This arrangement positions the central ring of EncFtn directly above the pore at the five-fold symmetry axis of the encapsulin shell and highlights a potential route for the entry of iron into the encapsulin and towards the active site of EncFtn.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural docking analysis and proposes a functional mechanism.

claim: The presence of five FOCs per EncFtnsH decamer and the fact that the icosahedral encapsulin nanocage can hold up to twelve decameric EncFtn means they can achieve a high rate of iron mineralization across the entire nanocompartment.
source: The presence of five FOCs per EncFtnsH decamer and the fact that the icosahedral encapsulin nanocage can hold up to twelve of decameric EncFtn between each of the internal five-fold vertices means that they can achieve a high rate of iron mineralization across the entire nanocompartment.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on structural analysis and stoichiometry calculations.

claim: The arrangement of multiple reaction centers in the encapsulin nanocompartment is reminiscent of classical ferritins, which have 24 FOCs distributed around the nanocage.
source: This arrangement of multiple reaction centers in a single protein assembly is reminiscent of classical ferritins, which has 24 FOCs distributed around the nanocage.
evidence: The claim is a comparison based on structural and functional analysis.

claim: The crystal structure of the T. maritima encapsulin shell protein has a negatively charged pore positioned to allow the passage of Fe2+ into the encapsulin.
source: The crystal structure of the T. maritima encapsulin shell protein has a negatively charged pore positioned to allow the passage of Fe2+ into the encapsulin and directs the metal towards the central, negatively charged hole of the EncFtn ring (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis of the encapsulin and EncFtn shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The five metal-binding sites on the interior of the EncFtn ring (Glu31/34-sites) may select for the Fe2+ ion and direct it towards their cognate FOCs.
source: The five metal-binding sites on the interior of the ring (Glu31/34-sites) may select for the Fe2+ ion and direct it towards their cognate FOCs.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on structural analysis of metal-binding sites.

claim: The oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ occurs within the FOC according to the model postulated by Honarmand Ebrahimi et al., 2012, in which the FOC acts as a substrate site through which iron passes.
source: We propose that the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ occurs within the FOC according to the model postulated by (Honarmand Ebrahimi et al., 2012) in which the FOC acts as a substrate site through which iron passes and is released on to weakly coordinating sites at the outer circumference of the protein (His57, Glu61 and Glu64), where it is able to form ferrihydrite minerals which can be safely deposited within the lumen of the encapsulin nanocompartment (Figure 14).
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on structural data and cited model.
